pr_title: scheduler: revert "Filter gated pods before calling isPodWorthRequeuing"
pr_body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The main part of PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124618 was adding this if check:

pkg/scheduler/internal/queue/scheduling_queue.go:

    movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue

         if pInfo.Gated {
              continue
         }

This was supposed to shortcut expensive work. But if a pod is gated because a plugin's PreEnqueue return false, then the event that caused movePodsToActiveOrBackoffQueue to be called must not be ignored for the pod. PreEnqueue has to be called for the pod again to check whether it is now scheduleable.

This affects DRA when using claim templates. This is independent from using classic DRA or structured parameters, in both cases a pod gets created, then the claim, and pod scheduling can only start once the claim exists.

Depending on timing, the scheduler sees the pod update (because the claim name is recorded in status) or the claim add first. If it first sees the pod update, the pod gets stuck because the claim is still unknown. Then when the claim add event is processed, the pod gets skipped because of the check above and remains stuck.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125223

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/125223: a recent optimization in the scheduler caused pods to get stuck.
```

/cc @gabesaba

I've added more logging to track down this problem in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/125313 and also included several other changes there in the hope that they might help, like https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/124595.

The underlying problem is that the following happens:
- pod gets created
- the PreEnqueue check fails for it because the claim for it has not been created yet (it's using a template)
- the claim controller creates the claim and stores its name in the pod status
- the scheduler detects an "Update event" for the pod, but PreEnqueue fails again because the claim has not been received yet
- the claim add event is received and processed, but does not trigger another scheduling attempt

My theory is that the two events (pod modified and claim added) are getting processed so close together that they conflict somehow. Is that plausible?

cc @sanposhiho @kerthcet @alculquicondor 

The "Update event" calls `sched.SchedulingQueue.Update`. The claim event calls `sched.SchedulingQueue.MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue` (from eventhandlers.go).

> Maybe the PreEnqueue logic should be reserved for things that don't depend on factors external to the Pod.

Let me show our usecase too, to vote -1 for this point..

We also use PreEnqueue in https://github.com/pfnet/scheduler-plugins/tree/master/plugins/gang (gang scheduling); PreEnqueue allows Pods to enter scheduling cycles iff _all_ Pods in the group are now ready to retry scheduling.
e.g., When gangA-pod1 is rejected by plugin-1 and when gangA-pod2 is rejected by plugin-2, we want to requeue all gangA Pods iff the scheduling queue observes some cluster events that could change the scheduling results of gangA-pod1 and gangA-pod2. (i.e., when QHints of plugin-1 and plugin-2 returns Queue for those Pods)

Our points to use PreEnqueue, not PreFilter, are -
- A better scheduling throughput: By filtering out Pods at PreEnqueue, we can prevent waste scheduling cycles for those Pods, improving a whole scheduling throughput of the scheduler.
- Prevent too long backoff: If we rejected gang Pods at PreFilter, their backoff time would get too long very easily. PreEnqueue is the only possible way we can filter out Pods without demanding their [penalty](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/09472b673d9e34b866fbd41c544887ba60d7ca7b/pkg/scheduler/framework/interface.go#L93-L95) (i.e., backoff).

If we look at such PreEnqueue only, it's more time-consuming than what the scheduling gate does, but if we look at an overal scheduling efficiency, it could be more efficient actually. And, it's a users' responsibility to take a balance between a demerit of time-consuming PreEnqueue and a merit of rich filtering with PreEnqueue.

So,
> I don't quite like it, because it introduces something specific about SchedulingGates into the "generic" scheduler logic.

to me, the reason doesn't make enough sense to limit PreEnqueue's usage as you said, forcing the usage not to depend on things apart from the pod itself. That'd be a big limitation, only considering the scheduling gate plugin, and requires an enough reason.

We have a similar approach to @sanposhiho. Our pre-enqueue is light weight and defaults to blocking a pod until we have done our processing. The default scheduler then is allowed to handle these pre-processed pods. Our primary goal is to prevent the backoff inside the default scheduler.
We enforce quotas in the scheduler, that could cause longer wait times for a pod has until quota is available. If we do not have pre-enqueue those pods will be penalised. That backoff caused major issues for us. We no longer have that problem. 

When we run in plugin mode we cannot schedule more pods than the default scheduler can handle. We are able to "release" enough pods via our pre-enqueue to not have any impact on the default scheduler throughput. Our scheduling cycle to pre-process pods runs independently out of sync of the default scheduler.

I thought about this weeks ago, the root cause here is **scheduling is coupled with requeueing**, specifically, the **activeQ**, scheduling cycle cares nothing about the other queues, so if we can make activeQ decoupled with two phases, the scheduling performance can improve a lot. Moreover, if requeueing becomes more and more complex in the future, it will occupy more time that the scheduling cycle should have. Well.. this beyonds the scope of preEnqueue extension point, but I think it values.

So I drafted a model here:
- make activeQ a object store rather than a queue, it can be a map then, accelerate the GET/UPDATE/DELETE OP.
- maintain a new ToScheduleQ (heap like today's activeQ), this is for the real scheduling, we'll sync the elements from activeQ to ToScheduleQ via a block channel. Considering `Pop` is quick, will not hold the lock for a long time, so synchronization performance will not be slow. 
- Then in the before we'll lock the `Pop` for the whole time of `movePodsToSchedulingQueue`, but now, only for the `write-to-the-ToScheduleQ`, it's much shorter.

Just to analyze a different option: locking twice when processing events:
1. Lock once to list all the pods that are in the queue (this could be a read lock)
2. Process PreEnqueue, scheduling hints and so on, without any lock.
3. Lock again (write this time) to move all the pods that need to be moved between queues.

The problem is that, between step 1 and 3, the scheduler could requeue additional pods, which could be made schedulable by the event. So this option doesn't work. Unless I missed something?

A reminder of our goal: we are trying to optimize for the case where scheduling is successful (pods can be bound), while we have many gated pods.

> Just to analyze a different option
...
The problem is that, between step 1 and 3, the scheduler could requeue additional pods, which could be made schedulable by the event. 

I think we probably can solve the problem actually.

So, the problem in the twice-lock approach, in details, is:

1. All events, which have happened until `AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent`, are stored in `inFlightEvents`
2. `AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent` (`addUnschedulableWithoutQueueingHint`) runs QHints for those past events.
  a. 💥  Between (2) and (3), the event handler receives an event and the queue handles it. This event may make the Pod schedulable.
3. The queue doesn't find any events that could make the Pod schedulable and puts the Pod back to unschedQ.

The point is there's a moment between (2) and (3). 
Currently, between (2) and (3), no event could be handled because `AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent` takes lock that the event handling (`MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue`) also requires. 
But, if we took the twice-lock approach, 💥 could happen.

One solution towards this problem is that we put the pod anyway in unschedQ first, and then handle `inFlightEvents`. i.e., `AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent` would be:

1. `AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent` always put the Pod into unschedQ first.
2. It runs QHints for `inFlightEvents`.
3. If it find the Pod should be moved to activeQ/backoffQ, then moves it from unschedQ. otherwise it just keeps the Pod in unschedQ.

In this way, there's no moment at all that could miss the events.
All events that have happened during the scheduling cycle are handled as `inFlightEvents`. And, all events that have happened during running `AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent` are handled in `MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue` side (as we put the Pod in unschedQ)
There could be events that are handled twice (in `MoveAllToActiveOrBackoffQueue` and in `AddUnschedulableIfNotPresent` as `inFlightEvents`), but that should be OK.
